items.title: SIMQ: A Single Graph-based Index for Multi-Vector Query
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness by representing documents as sets of token-level vectors and scoring via MaxSim, but their high computational cost limits scalability to large corpora. Existing approximate methods face fundamental bottlenecks: centroid interaction matrix approaches require computing a full matrix at every query and rely on GPU-accelerated clustering, while data-oblivious compression methods yield unstable recall that requires repeated compensation. We propose SIMQ (Single graph Index for Multi-vector Query), a framework that bridges single-vector graph indices and multi-vector retrieval through data-aware sampling-based clustering and per-token graph navigation, simultaneously bypassing all aforementioned bottlenecks. SIMQ organizes all token vectors into fine-grained clusters via data-aware sampling, builds a single graph index over cluster centroids independently of PLAID's residual representation, and approximates the MaxSim score through per-token graph search without materializing any interaction matrix or relying on GPU acceleration. We provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a manifold assumption and successful cell retrieval, data-aware partitioning has a smaller expected approximation error than a data-oblivious partition. Building on this foundation, SIMQ+ further introduces count-based scoring and a dynamic candidate set to improve robustness across varying query conditions. Experiments on five benchmarks compare recall, throughput, and construction time against several baselines, primarily on CPU; large-scale PLAID k-means centroids are built on a separate GPU machine. SIMQ has been integrated into VSAG, an Ant Group's open-source vector search library.

items.title: MoL-SQL: A Controlled Benchmark for Mixture-of-Language Text-to-SQL
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems are usually built and evaluated under a monolingual assumption, yet in international applications users often query databases stored in a different language. Existing multilingual benchmarks mostly translate only the question without aligning schema and value entities, so they can neither locate the source of an accuracy drop nor rule out translation errors. Hence, we introduce MoL-SQL, a benchmark for mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL that switches the languages of the question, schema, and stored values independently while keeping each task fixed, and grades every cross-lingual entity mapping into four difficulty levels. We migrate five Text-to-SQL benchmarks of different domains and source languages through a unified alignment pipeline that builds a shared cross-lingual entity map, migrates each database with its constraints, rewrites the gold SQL under execution-equivalence checks, and regenerates the question from the verified SQL, keeping all language versions of a task aligned in entities, intent, and execution result. MoL-SQL provides two splits: MoL-Full (16,892 samples) for overall evaluation and MoL-Cube (3,840 samples) covering every language combination to isolate question, schema, and value effects. Experiments with eight LLMs and four families of Text-to-SQL methods show that schema and value languages have distinct effects, with stored values costing up to 23 points, and that these effects mainly stem from cross-lingual entity mapping. Neither question translation nor additional reasoning narrows the value gap, whereas access to target-database values substantially reduces it, indicating that mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL benefits most from language-aware context grounding.

items.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

items.title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

items.title: Revisiting Index Performance under High Cache-Miss Penalties
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern data-intensive applications often query very large datasets, making index performance critical. Recent index structures exploit the fine-grained access capabilities of emerging storage devices such as DCPMM and CXL. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate indexes in isolation using saturated, closed-loop workloads that emphasize maximum throughput. Such workloads favor highly concurrent designs while overlooking the application work that follows an index lookup and competes for cache, memory bandwidth, and CPU resources. We present AuxBench - a microbenchmark that evaluates indexes as auxiliary access paths within larger application workloads. Using AuxBench, we evaluate four byte-addressable indexes under controlled post-lookup memory activity, concurrency, and request arrival patterns. Our experiments show that post-lookup memory activity can change the relative performance of competing indexes, that concurrency-oriented designs may lose their advantages when substantial application work is introduced, and that time-varying request arrivals can produce severe tail latency near saturation. These findings demonstrate why index-only benchmarks may not adequately predict performance in larger application workloads

items.title: Pelorus: Warped-Product Graph Indexing for Hyperbolic Vector Search
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings capture hierarchical relations, but million-scale approximate nearest neighbor search must reconcile geodesic fidelity with memory efficiency. Flat inner-product indices distort order across radial shells, while native hyperbolic graphs repeatedly access full-precision vectors or quantize coordinates with singular conformal scales. We present Pelorus, a warped-product proximity-graph index for hyperbolic vector search. Pelorus separates unquantized FP32 radial and conformal scalars from scale-invariant 2-bit spherical directional codes and defers full-vector FP64 evaluation to a compact reranking tail. A conformal distortion analysis motivates orthogonal-projection debiasing, purity-gated tangent-cone residuals, and Conformal Jacobian gating. QuadriPrune allocates edges across geodesic fibers, same-shell rings, and radial elevators, with spanning-tree chord swaps restoring entry reachability. A single-page record layout and carry-save AVX2 kernel accelerate traversal. Across eight real and synthetic benchmarks on AMD EPYC 9654, Pelorus builds Cohere-1M indices 5.44x faster than full-precision polar graphs on 32 threads, reducing hot navigation memory to 517.0 MB. At 99% Recall@10, it improves Cohere-1M throughput by 4.30x on one thread and 6.31x on 24 threads, and delivers 53,483 QPS on MERU-1M. On clustered narrow shells, tangent-cone residuals raise recall from 34.22% to 99.385%, while isotropic narrow-shell stress tests expose remaining recall limits.

items.title: Errpedia: Is Your Exact $k$-NN Vector Search Really Exact?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) vector search is a common feature of vector libraries and database systems. It serves applications that require exact results and provides the ground truth for evaluating approximate search. However, floating-point rounding and overflow can cause an exact search to return mathematically incorrect top-$k$ result sets. These errors can go unnoticed and affect downstream tasks that rely on exact results. We present Errpedia, a purpose-built dataset for testing the numerical correctness of exact vector search. Errpedia contains 1,616 queries across 21 error categories, with ground truth independently verified using exact rational arithmetic. We evaluate 20 widely used library and database configurations and find that every tested configuration returns mathematically incorrect top-10 result sets on at least 1 applicable query. Failures include misranking nearly equidistant vectors and returning incomplete results: 1 library omits all 10 exact matches to a query, and several systems return fewer than $k$ neighbors. We release Errpedia as a reproducible benchmark for developers and researchers to test their implementations. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/dynos01/errpedia.

items.title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

items.title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark. Compared with diffusion-based estimation, FACE requires substantially fewer sampling steps while achieving superior or comparable estimation accuracy, reducing inference time and computational cost. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of flow matching for accurate, pilot-efficient, and computationally efficient mmWave MIMO channel estimation.

items.title: Regularized Score Centering
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.
